Genesis. Genesis is the first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Old Testament, narrating humanity's origins, God's creation, the fall of humanity through sin, and the patriarchal history of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Written in ancient Hebrew and traditionally attributed to Moses, though scholars date it to multiple sources spanning centuries, it establishes foundational myths, genealogies, and covenants central to Judaism and Christianity.

The book opens with the Creation narrative in which God creates the heavens and earth in six days and rests on the seventh, establishing the Sabbath. This ordering reflects ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian cosmologies reframed through Israelite monotheism. Adam and Eve, the first humans, are created in God's image and placed in the Garden of Eden. Their disobedience in eating the forbidden fruit introduces sin, shame, and mortality, explaining human suffering and death.

Noah and the Great Flood represent God's judgment on human wickedness and the destruction of all but the righteous. The story reflects ancient Mesopotamian flood narratives like the Gilgamesh Epic, adapted into Israelite theology. Abraham is introduced as the ancestor chosen by God to found a great nation. His covenant with God, including circumcision and promised descendants, establishes the special relationship between God and the Israelite people.

Isaac and Jacob continue the patriarchal line. Jacob is renamed Israel after wrestling with an angel, and his twelve sons become the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel. Joseph's story—sold into slavery, rising to power in Egypt, and reuniting with his family—concludes Genesis and transitions to the Exodus narrative, explaining how Israelites came to live in Egypt.

Genesis contains diverse literary forms: creation myths, genealogies, narrative stories, poetry, and legal material, suggesting compilation from multiple sources over centuries. Modern scholars identify Priestly, Jahwist, and Elohist sources within the text.
